ch: Mucosal and submucosal outpouchings through the muscular wall without inflammation
questions.exp: Diverticulosis refers to mucosal and submucosal herniations through weak points in the muscularis propria without inflammation.

questions.q: The most common location of diverticulitis is the:
questions.exp: The sigmoid colon is the most common site because of its smaller lumen and higher intraluminal pressures.

questions.q: Which mechanism most commonly initiates acute diverticulitis?
ch: Obstruction of a diverticulum with subsequent microperforation
questions.exp: Obstruction by a fecalith or stool leads to bacterial overgrowth, microperforation, and inflammation.

questions.q: Which combination is the classic presentation of uncomplicated diverticulitis?
questions.exp: The classic presentation is left lower quadrant pain with fever and leukocytosis.
CT with IV contrast is the diagnostic gold standard.
Inflamed diverticula with pericolic fat stranding are characteristic.
Abscesses >3-5 cm are generally treated with drainage and antibiotics.

questions.q: Which statement about antibiotics is correct?
ch: Mild uncomplicated disease in selected immunocompetent patients may be managed without routine antibiotics
questions.exp: Modern guidelines recommend selective antibiotic use in carefully selected uncomplicated cases.

questions.q: Which Hinchey stage represents generalized fecal peritonitis?
questions.exp: Stage IV is generalized fecal peritonitis and requires emergency management.

questions.q: Which is the first priority in suspected bowel obstruction?
ch: Resuscitation with IV fluids, bowel rest, and decompression
questions.exp: Initial management focuses on resuscitation, NPO status, and decompression.

questions.q: The most common cause of adult small bowel obstruction is:
questions.exp: Adhesions are the leading cause of adult SBO.

questions.q: Which finding raises concern for strangulation?

Proximal SBO usually causes early vomiting.

questions.q: Perforation risk rises once cecal diameter exceeds approximately:
questions.exp: Marked cecal dilation increases perforation risk.
Stable adhesive SBO may undergo a monitored nonoperative trial.

questions.q: Which medication class should generally be avoided in fixed mechanical obstruction?
questions.exp: Prokinetics may worsen a fixed obstruction.

questions.q: Which complication most directly results from impaired bowel perfusion?
questions.exp: Reduced perfusion leads to ischemic bowel injury.

questions.q: Which description most accurately characterizes ulcerative colitis?
ch: Transmural inflammation occurring anywhere from mouth to anus
Continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum and confined to the colon
Patchy inflammation involving the terminal ileum but sparing the colon
Granulomatous inflammation limited to the small intestine
Perianal fistulizing disease with skip lesions
questions.exp: Ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum, extends proximally in a continuous pattern, is limited to the mucosa/submucosa, and remains confined to the colon.
why: Transmural, mouth-to-anus involvement describes Crohn's disease.
Patchy terminal ileal disease is more typical of Crohn's disease.
Granulomas may occur in Crohn's disease and are not limited to the small intestine.
Perianal fistulas and skip lesions strongly favor Crohn's disease.

questions.q: Which complication is most directly explained by the transmural nature of Crohn's disease?
questions.exp: Full-thickness inflammation can penetrate adjacent tissues, producing fistulas, abscesses, and strictures.
why: Tenesmus is associated with rectal inflammation and commonly favors ulcerative colitis.
Superficial bleeding is consistent with mucosal ulceration in ulcerative colitis.
Loss of haustra produces the chronic ulcerative-colitis lead-pipe appearance.
Continuous proctitis is an ulcerative-colitis pattern.

questions.q: Which presentation most strongly favors ulcerative colitis over Crohn's disease?
ch: Right lower-quadrant pain with a draining perianal fistula
Weight loss with terminal ileal inflammation
Bloody diarrhea with urgency and tenesmus
Recurrent bowel obstruction from a fibrotic stricture
questions.exp: Bloody diarrhea, urgency, and tenesmus are characteristic of rectal and colonic mucosal inflammation in ulcerative colitis.
why: Right lower-quadrant pain and perianal fistulae favor Crohn's disease.
Terminal ileal involvement is a classic Crohn's distribution.
Fibrotic strictures result from transmural Crohn's disease.
Intra-abdominal abscesses are a penetrating Crohn's complication.

questions.q: Which test is considered confirmatory for inflammatory bowel disease and helps distinguish ulcerative colitis from Crohn's disease?
questions.exp: Ileocolonoscopy with biopsy confirms IBD and demonstrates continuous friable mucosa in ulcerative colitis versus skip lesions, cobblestoning, and possible granulomas in Crohn's disease.
why: p-ANCA and ASCA are supportive but not diagnostic.
Ultrasound is not the confirmatory test in the source protocol.
Fecal calprotectin indicates intestinal inflammation but does not establish subtype by itself.
CT enterography evaluates small-bowel Crohn's disease and complications but does not replace biopsy confirmation.

questions.q: A patient with known IBD presents with worsening diarrhea while receiving immunosuppressive therapy. Which step should occur before escalating immunosuppression?
ch: Order ASCA testing to confirm an acute flare
Start an antidiarrheal agent before further evaluation
Schedule colectomy regardless of IBD subtype
questions.exp: Stool cultures, ova and parasite testing, and C. difficile evaluation should precede escalation of immunosuppression; CMV may also require consideration in a severe flare.
why: Steroids may induce remission but should not be started reflexively before excluding infection.
ASCA is supportive of Crohn's disease but does not distinguish infection from active inflammation.
Antidiarrheals may be dangerous when toxic megacolon or severe colitis is possible.
Surgery depends on subtype, severity, complications, and response to treatment.

questions.q: Which statement about corticosteroid therapy in IBD is correct?
ch: Corticosteroids are preferred for lifelong maintenance
Corticosteroids are used to induce remission during moderate or severe flares
Corticosteroids are curative in ulcerative colitis
Corticosteroids prevent postoperative Crohn's recurrence indefinitely
Corticosteroids should be stopped abruptly once symptoms improve
questions.exp: Prednisone or budesonide may be used to induce remission during an active flare.
why: Corticosteroids are not maintenance therapy because of cumulative toxicity.
Colectomy - not corticosteroid therapy - can be curative for ulcerative colitis.
Crohn's disease may recur after surgery, and steroids do not provide indefinite prevention.
Systemic steroids generally require tapering and should not be stopped abruptly.

questions.q: A patient with moderate-to-severe IBD is being evaluated for immunomodulator and biologic therapy. Which assessment set is most appropriate?
ch: Latent tuberculosis screening, hepatitis B testing, CBC/TPMT assessment, and exclusion of active infection
Serum amylase, lipase, and troponin testing
Immediate biologic treatment without laboratory evaluation
questions.exp: Appropriate preparation includes latent TB and hepatitis B screening before biologics, CBC and TPMT assessment when thiopurines are considered, and exclusion of active infection.
why: ASCA alone neither confirms Crohn's disease nor establishes treatment safety.
These tests do not constitute the standard IBD immunosuppression workup.
Endoscopy is important, but treatment safety also requires infectious and laboratory screening.
Biologic therapy can reactivate serious infection and should not begin without appropriate evaluation.

questions.q: A hospitalized patient with ulcerative colitis develops fever, tachycardia, marked abdominal distension, and colonic dilation greater than 6 cm. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
ch: Toxic megacolon requiring urgent medical and surgical evaluation
Mild ulcerative-colitis flare appropriate for outpatient mesalamine alone
questions.exp: Colonic dilation greater than 6 cm with fever, tachycardia, and distension is toxic megacolon and requires urgent multidisciplinary management.
why: The systemic toxicity and colonic dilation indicate a life-threatening complication, not a functional disorder.
This presentation is too severe for outpatient treatment.
Laxatives, antidiarrheals, and opioids may worsen dangerous colonic dilation.
Terminal ileal strictures produce obstructive Crohn's symptoms but do not describe diffuse toxic colonic dilation.

questions.q: A patient with terminal ileal Crohn's disease is at increased risk for which combination?
ch: Vitamin B12 deficiency, gallstones, and calcium-oxalate kidney stones
Vitamin C excess, uric-acid stones, and hypercalcemia
Iron overload, cholesterol deficiency, and nephrotic syndrome
Folate toxicity, pancreatic cancer, and cystinuria
Vitamin A excess, pigment stones, and respiratory alkalosis
questions.exp: Terminal ileal disease can impair vitamin B12 and bile-salt absorption, contributing to B12 deficiency, gallstones, and enteric hyperoxaluria with calcium-oxalate stones.
why: This combination is not associated with terminal ileal Crohn's disease.
Iron deficiency - not overload - may occur in IBD.
These are not the expected terminal ileal complications described in the module.
The listed abnormalities do not follow from terminal ileal malabsorption.

questions.q: A patient has had extensive ulcerative colitis for nine years and also has primary sclerosing cholangitis. Which management principle is most appropriate?
ch: Delay colorectal cancer surveillance until symptoms worsen
Begin or continue surveillance colonoscopy because risk increases with disease duration, with earlier surveillance warranted in PSC
Use corticosteroids indefinitely to prevent colorectal cancer
Reassure the patient that colectomy cannot cure ulcerative colitis
Use ASCA levels as the primary colorectal cancer screening test
questions.exp: Colorectal cancer risk rises with long-standing colonic IBD. Surveillance generally begins at approximately eight years, and PSC warrants earlier surveillance.
why: Surveillance is based on disease duration and extent, not the onset of new symptoms.
Corticosteroids are not used indefinitely for cancer prevention.
Colectomy can cure the intestinal disease of ulcerative colitis.
ASCA is a supportive Crohn's serology, not a colorectal cancer screening test.
